speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to support this private member's motion to allow residential taxes and rental payments to be deductible from income taxes, put forward by my colleague the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz). This measure is long overdue and it is one that I have personally advocated for some time. I strongly support the principle that a proportion of municipal property taxes should be deductible from federal income taxes and that comparable tax relief should be extended to tenants.
The Canadian family's dream of owning a single family dwelling is fading faster than ever. Housing costs have soared in the past few years at rates that were thought inconceivable a few years earlier. The cost of borrowing money is prohibitive. Whether the housing crisis is one of shortage or price is of little consequence to the average Canadian taxpayer who must be making at least $17,000 annually to even obtain a mortgage before he is able to consider purchasing a home; otherwise, he is forced to live in an apartment or row housing.
Approximately 70 per cent of Canadians want to own a single family dwelling on a decent sized lot. Today, in Canadian cities, less than 5 per cent of the population can afford to buy a home and many of these must pay up to half their income in mortgage payments. When one knows of such situations it is very easy to understand why this motion should be accepted. Another reason apart from helping prospective and recent home buyers is the astronomical municipal tax rate in many cities. The people in Winnipeg are a classic example of this. Since unicity was forced on them, the municipal rates have risen in unprecedented jumps. These people are in urgent need of some tax relief.
There are more reasons for this motion being accepted. Every Canadian should, as a right, be able to obtain and live in suitable, reasonable-cost housing with the amenities of landscape. Within the natural constraints of geography and necessary economic and social limitations, the aim of government policy should be to generate sufficient housing stock of various forms so that all Canadians may exercise their freedom of choice as to the style and tenure of housing in which they live.
Canada's extremely high inflation rate of the last half decade has been a main instigator of the present price crisis. The government continues to blame inflation on other countries, but in the housing sector that just will not wash because in most houses presently being built there is nothing imported other than the thermostat control. This excuse is even less plausible than in the other sectors of the economy. The government owes some relief to the people hard hit by these price rises.
The motion before us would not only help alleviate the plight of new home buyers but present home owners as well, people who are being taxed to death by all levels of government. I cannot express too strongly, Madam Speaker, the necessity for this motion to be accepted by the House so that the government is steered into taking some definitive action toward clearing up this very serious situation.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTAL PAYMENTS BE DEDUCTIBLE UP TO MAXIMUM OF $300 PER YEAR
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the arguments advanced by my colleague the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) who introduced this motion, and also the hon. member opposite who just spoke. The motion is something of an old chesnut. It usually takes the form of allowing deductions for interest payments on mortgages- that is not included in this motion-or tax payments to municipalities, usually with the aim of encouraging home ownership. There are two objections that have traditionally been raised against this kind of motion. One, that it discriminates in favour of the higher income groups, so my colleague has put a ceiling of $300 on the claim. The second objection is that it does not do much for those who rent, so he has allowed an equivalent, offsetting deduction for tenants.
I have the greatest respect for my hon. colleague, Madam Speaker, but it is my contention that by introducing these qualifications he has failed to ask himself the basic question. What is he trying to do by the motion? In my opinion, the motion fails to achieve the basic purpose that he has in mind. Two basic principles were put forward by the two previous speakers. One was that it will encourage home ownership-I want to come back to that- by making the deduction available to every taxpayer who qualifies, regardless whether they rent or own a home. I fail to see that it gives any incentive whatsoever to home ownership. It considers tenants and owners on the same basis for tax deduction purposes.
When we talk about tax relief, let us look at the principle behind it and ask if this is the best means of giving such relief. It is my contention that there are more fair and more equitable means of doing so and I think they should be considered in priority to the motion before us.
Let us return to the first proposition, that it will encourage home ownership. The Department of Finance has indicated that something like $1,800 million would be lost to the treasury if such motions were implemented for the current tax year. If such a sum of money were to be lost to the government in revenues, there would inevitably have to be adjustments in taxes in other sectors.
Let us ask ourselves the basic question: what do we hope to achieve by the measure? The argument is that it will encourage home ownership. Let us consider that in relation to the present tax laws, taking taxpayer A and taxpayer B for comparison. Taxpayer A puts $40,000 into stocks and bonds and trust income; taxpayer B puts $40,000 into a home and leaves it there. Taxpayer A has to report the income on his investments of, say, 10 per cent per year and so has to include $4,000 per year in his taxable income. The owner of the home, taxpayer B, does not have to compute the economic rent of living in the home in his income. Our tax laws do not call for that, although the tax laws of some other countries such as the United Kingdom, do.
The second advantage that the owner of a house has under our present tax laws is freedom from capital gains tax on disposal of his principal place of residence, and that is a substantial advantage. The owner of investments does not have such an advantage when disposing of them, but is subject to the full capital gains tax. It is my contention that if the federal government wanted to go into the

Mr. Speaker, the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) indicate once again the lack of comprehension increasingly apparent on that side of the House concerning the magnitude of the housing crisis confronting this country. I have been most interested in the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz). I hope that the members of his own party have been equally attentive, particularly the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner).
Obviously, the hon. member for Parkdale is concerned with the high cost of shelter in this country, and well he might be. The cost of new housing is well beyond the capability of all but a very minute per cent of the Canadian public. The cost of existing housing for the majority of Canadians is eating up far more than the 25 per cent of total income considered appropriate by the Canadian Council on Social Development and by CMHC in their guidelines for AHOP eligibility. It cannot be reiterated too often that the residential construction industry is in a critical situation. Housing starts have fallen by 50 per cent from a year ago, down to some 160,000 projected annually. Mortgage rates are zooming toward new highs, currently

Residential Taxes
at 11 per cent and estimated to continue rising. Mortgage funds, particularly with the trust companies, have all but dried up.
Lenders have stopped lending. Builders have stopped building. Buyers have stopped buying. Meanwhile, the formation of new household units continues at an annual rate of 230,000. Therefore, we have looming before us a desperate situation in the housing field. Family units are increasing, housing starts are dropping. The shortage of accommodation becomes ever more critical. What social problems and unrest that presages! The proposal we have before us, while laudable, will do little to alleviate this situation. The deduction of property taxes or rental payments to a maximum of $300 for income tax purposes will do little to stimulate the badly sagging residential construction industry. Such measures will have little effect on the desperate housing shortage. They will, of course, have no bearing at all on the high cost of land or the high cost of money, two of the principal factors in the present crisis.
The government seems intent on allowing interest rates in general and mortgage rates in particular to rise, and this at a time when its stated intention is to stimulate the economy. The Bank of Canada is following this very formula at the present time. Obviously, rising interest rates will have the effect of dampening, not stimulating, the economy. These contradictory objectives are typical of the confused fiscal policies now being put forward by this government, and nowhere is this more apparent than in the field of housing. Will the government not see its way clear to giving the taxpayer some relief by allowing at least a proportion of the current high interest mortgage costs as a deduction for income tax purposes? That at least would serve to bring interests rates down.
During the election campaign last year, my leader put forward a proposal to bring down interest rates by controlling inflation, but persons who have taken on mortgages at these excessive rates will continue to suffer for some years to come. In order to alleviate at least in part the harsh impact of these high interest rates on home owners, we propose to permit taxpayers to deduct interest in excess of 8 per cent on a first mortgage on their principal residence. This was the approximate rate in effect when Mr. Trudeau first began to mismanage the economy.

Essentially, this is a taxation matter, not essentially one to stimulate the housing market. It is on this ground that the suggestion lacks merit. The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) has set out in perceptive detail the difficulties which would flow from the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Park-dale. The broad nature of the taxing proposal is such that it would bring no benefit whatever to those in the lower income brackets, while benefitting to an appreciable extent those in the higher income brackets about whom the hon. lady is probably less concerned.
The fact is that a tax-free investment such as a home can represent, in the hands of a person in the higher income tax brackets enjoying a maximum of a $300 deduction from his or her income tax, would be an appreciable advantage as compared to, say, a pensioner living in a home he owns and having no taxable income and not enjoying a similar benefit.
The cost of the program is estimated as being in the area of $1.8 billion a year. We would either have to find this money elsewhere out of the taxpayers' pockets or reduce programs in other directions, possibly in directions which are already stimulating the housing market. So, on the taxation principle that we do not provide a taxpayer with a deduction in respect of personal expenses, the measure would fall on this point alone.
As to a person living in rental accommodation, there are a variety of provincial schemes which endeavour to provide low rental accommodation for people with moderate incomes. These programs would be distorted if a further reduction for rental were permitted on whatever tax these people might have to pay. So the various objectives do not, in my judgment, go to the question of attempting to
Residential Taxes
resolve the problem created by the heavy burden of taxation being felt by everyone due to the large amount of governing being done in this country.
With regard to the fact that there is no provision for integrating taxation to the level I should like to see, I suggest it would be far better to have a system under the Income Tax Act to take better note of mortgage interest and municipal taxes, embodying them at the income tax level so that people could have their taxes reduced by having their exemption raised. By this method the government could raise personal exemptions to benefit those who were not in the high income tax brackets.
I think it is really with respect to the nature of the solution offered by the hon. member for Parkdale that the only criticism lies, not in his objective. It is directed to the inequity of the benefit, to the fact that only those in the higher income tax brackets would benefit. I know there are a variety of stimulative measures that the government has already taken in previous budgets in an endeavour to keep the housing industry at a high level of activity, and particularly in these days to increase housing starts. But I suggest more needs to be done.
I hope that in his forthcoming budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) will take note of these needs, and will endeavour to provide stimulative measures to revive the housing industry, an industry that is so important to the economy and which benefits all levels of income earners in Canada. In conclusion, may I simply say it is not the objectives of the hon. member's suggestion with which I quarrel; rather it is with his method.

We heard some scoffing at the $500 grant. It should be pointed out to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), when speaking in Toronto on May 1, pointed out that there has been an enthusiastic response to our offer of a $500 grant to all first time purchasers of new, modestly priced houses. He pointed out that we have now paid out some $7 million in home-owner grants to about 14,000 families. These are families who would not have been helped had it not been for this particular piece of legislation.
Hon. members scoffed at the Assisted Home Ownership Plan. I would point out in that respect, as the minister did in his speech, that it is probably the most popular housing program ever introduced in Canada. It should be pointed out that more than $124 million has been allocated in AHOP loans to Canadian families. If this continues at the same rate we will have allocated more than $340 million by the end of this year. These are facts. It is easy to get up and say things are not being done, but this $124 million will blossom into $340 million through this single piece of legislation.

Western Grain Stabilization

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-41, respecting the stabilization of net proceeds from the production and sale of western grain and to amend certain statutes in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Baker (Grenville-Carleton) (p.	).

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was appealing to the House to have this particular bill set back so that the standing committee could have an opportunity to go to western Canada and hear representations from the farm producers. It is not sufficient to have a few briefs submitted by the executives of a few farm organizations because this bill, in its original form, did not meet with favour.
I pointed out that in western Canada there is a great distrust of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), which he brought upon himself simply because of the way he handled other legislation and other problems. He has injected himself, whether voluntarily or on the insistence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), into areas which are not considered to be within his domain as a minister. I pointed out the area of transportation about which we are very concerned.
It is interesting that after several years' delay the minister should suddenly slip in this bill just at about the time farmers are preparing to go on the land. That in itself is an indication that there is something about which the farmers should be aware. Every member of this House must be aware that when the farmers are on the land they are busy and do not have any time to be concerned about policy making or carrying on discussions. After all that time the minister suddenly decides to bring into the House a bill which he states is part of the government's over-all policy. No farmer will take the time while he is on the land to make representations, and yet there has been no effort until now to introduce this bill.
I am sure the farmers can live without this bill for another few months, or forever if it is not improved. Some of the problems in the original bill have not been corrected. The bill contains much window dressing. There are many problems. I have already mentioned the $100 million prize offered, but since then we know that $130 million has been collected. The question of regional consideration is not taken into account. The minister, in dealing briefly with this, said they looked at it but were not satisfied and required further information. What guarantee is there that a number of years from now they will still not have a solution?
In my proposal in respect of the original bill I said we should take into account the block system. We know that the Canadian Wheat Board manipulates grain movements through the block system. It is possible to have one area deliver more than another area simply because of the
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
manipulations of the Canadian Wheat Board. The minister says that we do not know the cost of production for individual areas. We ask why we cannot have a bill which takes into account the overall cost of production, but with regional pay-outs? We could give the government three, four, or five years to figure out a plan, and in the meantime work on the basis of the block system.
Since the minister has not even looked at that problem and has merely commented on it, I shall go one step further in view of the great problem in western Canada today. The smaller communities, as the minister is aware, are struggling for existence. One solution to their problem might be through the use of this legislation. We know the Canadian Wheat Board has a computer system by which every delivery point is known. We know exactly what the income is in every area where there is an elevator, and therefore the calculation can be made on the basis of every community. If the minister really wants to help these communities, this in his golden opportunity. I am sure all the people in the smaller communities would make this appeal. I say they should be given the opportunity.
Frost affects many areas locally. Frost may affect at one time only a few communities in a block. These are the communities that will be adversely affected, and they should receive the benefits of any stabilization. They should not have to wait for an area which has had bumper crops for a long period to have a failure, before they can obtain assistance. This is the type of question I should like the minister to answer. Having waited all these years, if we are to have a stabilization bill which will be effective on behalf of all these communities, why could we not wait a few more months, or even a few years, to accomplish this?
That is one of the big arguments at this particular time. Why would the minister overlook this? Why must the depressed areas subsidize the areas that have always had it good when it comes to delivery? They may have had good crops on a continual basis, but suddenly when the entire region suffers from a crop failure the better areas qualify for a payment. My area is one of those that suffer from snow, frost, flooding, grasshoppers, beetles. You name it, we have it. We are a frontier area. When it comes to disasters, we have all kinds of them. Often we have late crops, and in many cases we have poor quality crops. You can break sales down very simply. There are statistics available in the Wheat Board office in Winnipeg right now.
I did say that I had some 20 questions to put to the minister, but I do not know how many of them I will be able to put in the time available. Another question is: do we need this particular kind of plan? I am suggesting that this plan does not meet our requirements.
Then there is the question as to whether the plan should be mandatory. The minister made it possible for farmers to opt out after three years, but his department will not have the statistics until the three years are up. The minute you have the statistics, you are either in or out, and that is final. The minister should give the farmers an opportunity to consider the plan for a longer time. We will not gain
May 5, 1975

sufficient experience in three years. The clause as it stands now does not cover the situation adequately.
The next question is: why do we not take into account the entire cost of production? Even the income tax people recognize certain costs of producing grain as a legitimate deduction. The income tax people can be tough enough, but they recognize many of these costs as legitimate deductions, and yet the Minister of Justice himself tells us that he will not include those expenses that are included for income tax purposes. I say that the minister should take that into account.
Then, when it comes to considering averages, why must we take a backward look? Farmers are asking these questions. Why are we taking into account the average income over the past years? Nobody who works for a salary wants to sign a contract on the basis of his average income in the past five years. Surely to goodness the government should be forward looking these days. We know that inflation is with us, but the government has done nothing about it. If we make calculations, why should we not make them taking into account inflation? Even if you have to base the formula on the previous five years, you should add the rate of inflation that was experienced in the last five years.
If you take the cost of production into account, you must remember that today the dollar is not worth what it was two years ago. If you give the producer $100 today, you know as well as I do that he cannot purchase the same amount that he could two years ago. The cost of fertilizer went up three times. Why must we constantly look backward in agricultural matters? Why does agriculture not take its rightful place alongside other industries? Why must farmers be considered second or third rate citizens?
I have already mentioned the matter of payment on a regional basis. We take acts of God into account, but we must also consider acts of the minister with regard to regional economies. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) covered that question fully when he mentioned LIFT. The producers' income could be manipulated by the minister. What is the Wheat Board going to do once it collects the information? These are questions that have not been answered. Will they make decisions regarding grain deliveries and shipments out of those areas on the basis of the information they collect? Will they report incomes to the revenue department?
Why is it that the social insurance number has to be recorded in all transactions? Must the farmer have a third copy to submit to the Wheat Board, or whoever is administering the program, in all transactions, such as transactions regarding seed grain being purchased by one farmer from another farmer? Is Big Brother to look into all transactions? Why is the social insurance number mentioned in the bill before us, and why are farmers suspect? What will the minister do with that type of information?
Why must a farmer who happens to be in the elevator when the commissioner comes have to remain there until the commissioner is through with him? He may be dropping in for a social call, but the farmer has to remain there until the commissioner is satisfied that he has all the information. If he decides to keep the farmer there for the rest of the day, the farmer must stay. These are some of
Western Grain Stabilization
the questions the bill raises. What is the need for that type of control and authority? What kind of police state are we creating?

Why was that limitation put on? What is so sacred about $25,000? Perhaps that figure appealed to the minister at a time when the cost of wheat was $1.50, but it is no longer that.
Another question is with regard to the exclusion of certain farmers. Why can we not include all farmers? How does the farmer receive his overpayment? If, for example, he had an income of almost $25,000, and then, after a crop failure everywhere, how does he recover his overpayment.
Consider the bureaucracy. The minister said we will not have inspectors. If that is so, then how will he know how much grain is produced, and how will he know about transactions between farmers? How will he know whether or not I fed my grain to my cattle?

speechtext:
What plans are there to review the program after a few years? Why is it that we are making the same mistake we made with PFAA? Originally PFAA was set up on the basis of townships. Why must we go into large regions, and then find out several years later that farmers must come to government to beg them to amend the legislation, when we know that that is what they asked for a few years ago? Why must we make the same mistakes again in the hope that the farmers will come begging to the government to introduce amendments to the act? The government will then say to them, "Look what wonderful things we are doing for you."
Fortunately for the farmers the government changed the provisions under PFAA. The Conservative administration was in office at that time. Why is it we are starting on the wrong foot right from the beginning when we have waited for this legislation for a few years?
If the government is paying 4 per cent of the levy, why can we not put the 4 per cent into a crop insurance plan, for example, thus improving the plan so that it would benefit the farmers and so that everybody could operate his own scheme? There would be no need for policing other than we have now. Under the crop insurance scheme provincial governments have set up a system of inspection and they know how it operates. We could improve on that. We do not need another army checking into the operation.

May 5, 1975

I am afraid that this will bring about an army of inspectors, and that it will bring about an army of political inspectors. If the minister is setting up another Gardiner machine, I want to know why we need one. The farmers do not need one. Perhaps the minister does, but if we must levy 2 per cent to set up his political machine, we do not want it. These are the kinds of things about which farmers are asking.
I ask the minister what the total contribution from the federal treasury will be? In his speech he was only able to skim over a few figures. When farmers' levies for all the years are taken into account, when the years when farmers do not receive payment under this plan are taken into account, when it is considered that there will be years when payments will be lucrative for one area even though that area experiences a bumper crop, when income tax is deducted from these areas, much of that money will be coming back to the treasury.
We would like to know what the total federal involvement will be. What is the government pushing here? Is it coming through with a plan which will provide a larger income to the farmer, or is it suggesting that the total distribution of available funds will be really adequate? It may just be an imaginary figure the minister has dreamed up in the course of trying to sell this idea of stabilization. Are we going to be stabilized above poverty level? It appears that this will happen because we are not escalating incomes in accordance with the rate of inflation.
We ask whether this bill can be written in a less complex way. Lawyers have stood in this House, and one quoted certain sections of the bill. Anyone reading this bill would wonder what kind of formula is being drafted. If the Minister of Justice, with all the expertise he has in his department, cannot draft anything simpler than this, I wonder what chance any farmer will have to determine whether he is actually being overpaid. There is a clause in the bill which says that if a farmer is over paid, he should refund this money. How in the world is he supposed to figure out whether he is over paid? On the basis of this formula it would be pretty tough going. I am sure that if the minister's department cannot draft something simpler, we will have farmers involved in litigation. Lawyers in the courts will have a real field day trying to defend someone, but that is about the only benefit this bill might have.
The minister might also explain how this bill will affect, for example, the port of Churchill. If the government can manipulate grain according to the statistics it has, how will that area be affected? If we find certain economies, will we be trying to push for those developments in western Canada? Do we have to wait for the southern area, such as Assiniboia, Rosetown, Biggar, and other heavy growing areas for benefits? Perhaps we will have to wait for them to have a crop failure before we receive benefits. What is the advantage? What is the net result of this type of readjustment in the thinking of farmers as far as western development is concerned? How is the small community going to benefit where it has been manipulated in the past?
I already indicated, for example, where grain was shipped from Assiniboia to the port of Churchill, and not

grain coming from my area which is right next to the port of Churchill. Would that kind of manipulation stop? Why should we allow it to continue with this kind of bill? Can we not check some of these inadequacies in connection with transportation? How will it affect, for example, the plea to retain certain railways? If the minister cannot figure out what the cost of production is to determine the total cash flow, how are we going to present a case for retaining railways?
The minister admits that at the present time he is having a tough struggle. Some of these inquiries are being conducted by the Canadian Transport Commission. Will the CTC be able to give us some of these answers which up until now we have not received? What effect will a trucking system have on the total cost of production? There have been studies. There have been grain deliveries into Saskatoon for a unit train set up. If the minister does not have that information and he tells us that he needs another year or so to obtain it, we might be patient and wait for the answer before we proceed.
There are many questions in the minds of farmers, but they hear few explanations. They fear that the minister is imposing something on them and in such a way that it will not help small communities which are struggling and fast being written off. The minister could help if he so wanted. We should have these answers before we proceed. If there is a possibility of an answer, we should know that before we consider tampering with adjustments or amendments to clauses. I suggest that we need more information. If the minister has not obtained the information, the committee is prepared to travel to obtain some of the answers. After receiving those answers, or at least making an attempt, we will then be prepared to consider the bill clause by clause to see what advantages, if any, there are for western Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the grain industry has been debated on more than one occasion in this session. The Standing Committee on Agriculture has also spent a good deal of time discussing grain and grain related questions, but the bill before us is by far the most important and significant single piece of legislation dealing with grain farmers and the western grain industry which has been put forward in a long time.
There is a considerable body of legislation dealing with various aspects of the grain industry. I can mention the two price wheat system which we dealt with earlier. There was a good deal of time spent in committee, and I think it is still before the House at some stage. The cash advance legislation and deferral of cash delivery tickets are examples of grain legislation. We have seen a number of other policy developments in the last several years, not all of which have required legislation. I am thinking of the implementation of the block shipping system and the extension of credit facilities to the Canadian Wheat Board in order to assist it in obtaining greater foreign sales around the world, which it has done.
I think of the government purchase of hopper cars, the establishment of the Canada Grains Council, the establishment of the grains administration group, and perhaps
May 5, 1975

the most recent move in this direction, the election of the producer board of the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board. These have been good moves. They have been helpful and necessary, and the list is by no means complete. I could mention other situations that have been corrected and other policies that have been introduced.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski), who just took his seat, was speaking about what is going to happen to the municipal roads if any of the branch lines are abandoned. I should like to ask my hon. friend if he remembers how things were a few years ago when grain was bootlegged in the real producing areas of Saskatchewan-Yorkton, Kindersley, up into his area and into Meadow Lake in northern Saskatchewan. More grain was unnecessarily moved by trucks because of an outdated quota system inherited from Conservative times, than was moved by rail.
When the hon. member talks about the possible damage to roads because of some possible rail line abandonment, I ask him to remember the bootlegging situation. I am sure he is well aware of it because it is one glaring example of the policies we inherited from his party when they were in government. Improvements such as the block shipping system and other innovative policies have come about under the present minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board.
Hon. members opposite have been very critical of the minister in this debate. He has the job of tackling the problems and policies of the grain industry, and they seem to wonder why a Saskatchewan minister, and member of parliament from that province, should be given this responsibility which is vital to western Canada. Is that wrong? One would think so, listening to the critics in the official opposition and, to a lesser extent, in the New Democratic Party. I am not sure, and I am sure nobody else is, just what disturbs my hon. friends in the opposition, because there has not been any basic criticism of the minister's performance. We have not heard any factual criticism of his many achievements in regard to the problems of the grain industry. They often refer to the LIFT program, and there were some good and bad things about that program, but they do not mention the record movements of grain, record sales to China and other markets, and the record exports of barley.
They forget that in 1969 the total barley exports, including malting barley, were 22 million bushels, but three years later under this minister were over 200 million bushels. They forget these things when speaking of the minister's performance.
It may be that what opposition members are really critical of is the determination and capable manner in which this minister has gone about analysing and tackling the problems of the grain industry. His approach is new, and different to members opposite. They always have simplistic answers-the NDP says "set the guaranteed price" regardless of production or any other problems. As far as the Official Opposition is concerned, their approach is more flamboyant-give a $200 payment to everybody.
While I commend the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), a former minister of agriculture, for what he has done for the western grain industry, we must remember that his one big effort was a
Western Grain Stabilization
large sale to China some years ago, which has been surpassed more than once by the present minister in charge of the Wheat Board. Western Canadians in general, and farmers in particular, have been impressed with the minister's (Mr. Lang) dedication, determination, and performance, and with the analytical manner in which he has sought solutions to the problems of the grain industry.
Western grain farmers, and I am sure this is true also of farmers in other branches of agriculture, are much better informed of the problems in their own industry than heretofore. This has been brought about by a concerted and positive effort by this government and this minister. I strongly believe that if government, or government agencies, can provide farmers with facts and figures, collectively and individually they will make their own decisions and do much better than governments or any other kind of advice of experts passed on to them. The program of getting information out to producers is part of a policy begun by the present minister.
The history of Bill C-41 was discussed earlier in this debate by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) and others, Mr. Speaker. Both the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Mazankowski), and the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton), pointed out that there are other issues and concerns that directly involve the grain farmer, such as transportation, labour unrest- even the weather when moving grain through the mountains of western Canada. That is true, of course, but the aim of this bill is much deeper and is not concerned with the problem of boxcar shortage, rail line upgrading, labour disputes and so on. That is the income question, the good years and the bad years, the cycles which directly affect not only the grain growers but almost every other sector and every other group of people in western Canada.
The importance of these cycles and their tremendous effect on the western economy is a difficult thing for Canadians in other parts of the country to understand, I am sure. Not everybody appreciates the tremendous importance of the health and welfare of the grain industry, and the dependence of all other sectors of the economy on that industry.
Western provincial governments of all political stripes- and in the last 30 years in Saskatchewan there have only been two-have wrestled for years with the problems of rural depopulation. Parties of all political stripes have fought to stabilize growth of development, and many good and helpful programs have been developed to improve the living standards of people in smaller urban communities in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. There have been programs such as natural gas service to small communities across the prairies, water, sewer, and other services, but despite that we have seen the trend away from farms and small communities.
The people who remain have been helped, but the trend of grain producers forced off the farm by the ups and downs of their lives, has not been reversed. These policies have been joined by a federal program of aid to agricultural service centres which is putting $10 million into Saskatchewan alone, and a similar amount into the other two prairie provinces, but still this has not prevented the flow of population from prairie towns to larger centres either westward or eastward. It is not because these people want

May 5, 1975
Western Grain Stabilization
to leave, but because they need a stable job on a year round basis. They have not been able to find that in large areas of western Canada. They are dependent on a steady, stable cash income from the grain grower. This bill is aimed at that basic problem, whether it be lack of world markets, lack of ability to penetrate those markets as it has been before, reduced market prices, or increased costs of operating the farms.
I agree with the hon. member for Mackenzie that Bill C-41 is complex and complicated. In this regard it differs in a major way from Bill C-50 which we discussed in this House not so very long ago. However, I suggest to hon. members that you cannot have it both ways. Members opposite criticized Bill C-50 because it was not specific enough. It did not spell out cost indexing, and so on and so forth. In this bill the minister is trying to enshrine all these various aspects of the policy into legislation and have them written into law, leaving very little to regulation. You cannot have it both ways.
I do not pretend to understand all of the formulae spelled out in the bill. It will require some good, solid committee work on behalf of members of all parties to go into the mechanism of the bill. In this debate, however, we are dealing with the principle of the bill. The principle is one of providing a form of income stability for grain producers and, as a result, for the other tradesmen, the other people in the prairie basin.
Net income stability is one of the features of this bill. It was not one of the features of a similar bill put forward a few years ago. That was a valid criticism at that time. The minister corrected that in consultation with dozens of farm organizations and farmer groups which met and had some input into this bill.
This is not a floor-price policy. It is not a 90 per cent of the best five years' index as was Bill C-50. It is a different principle. The bill establishes a fund for income stability. As I indicated earlier, income stability for the grain farmer is the first step in creating greater stability for the prairies.
What does the bill do? Very simply, it is a plan whereby a fund is established. The fund gets money from two sources. From the farmer it gets 2 per cent of gross sales up to $25,000. As far as the contribution from the farmer is concerned, this represents a maximum of $500. It will be matched by the government of Canada, the taxpayer and the treasury putting 4 per cent into the fund. The hon. member for Mackenzie said the $25,000 figure is too low. I do not know. At the moment I do not think it is. However, that is not the principle we are debating in this bill.
For every $3 put into the fund, $1 is put in by the farmers and $2 by the taxpayers and treasury of Canada. Who is going to get that $3, and how? It will be the farmer, and only the farmer, who will get any money out of that fund. That should be easily understood.
I cannot understand why any member opposite would want to defer for further study a bill containing this kind of deal for the western farmer. It cannot help but be a good plan in principle. The farmer receives a cheque from the fund if the total net income from grain drops below a five year average.

Farmers and farm groups have been consulted. They have been discussing this bill and the principle of it for the past four of five years. To defer it for another six months is sheer nonsense. It clearly demonstrates the lack of any kind of policy on the part of members opposite.
Members opposite do not say what should be done about this bill, only to put it off for six months. They have had five years to think about it. They went through the last election campaign in western Canada without any great plans or policies, other than fixing prices and wages, and that did not work. They have had a little time since then. They now ask for another six months so that some of the experts and the farm members from western Canada can think up a better policy. Having already had five years, I do not think another six months will do them any good.
Members opposite are very concerned about getting this bill into committee and then hitting the road for, I presume, public hearings all over the west. Anyone who looks at this bill can see that that would be a very premature kind of move. The first job of the committee is to spend some time with the officials in order to study the details of the bill. The committee can then consider where and when it should travel. The committee should meet with producer groups, as has been done with regard to other somewhat similar pieces of legislation. We do not need to travel around the prairies for weeks or months to do that. The committee has an obligation to ensure that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Palliser Grain growers, the wheat pools and other groups are brought here and informed of this legislation so that they in turn can explain it to their members.
The principle of this bill is designed to meet one of the great concerns of western farmers since homestead days. I do not pretend that it will solve all of the income problems in the grain industry. No fund or policy could do that. Crop insurance will still be essential. But it is going to be an integral part of the scheme. I am sure the bill will need to be improved.
I agree with one of the main criticisms of members opposite that we have to look a little harder and a little further for a better approach to varying regions in order to reflect the actual situation over the broad geographic area in a better way than that provided in the bill.
The official opposition want to stall this bill. That is the only suggestion they have made. I suggest the amendment is sheer nonsense. It is petty politics. It is sheer personal antagonism against the minister for the sake of small-time political gamesmanship. They want to stall instead of getting this legislation in place.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Mackenzie said it will take a year or two to get some facts, figures and experience. How in the world are we going to get experience if we do not pass this legislation, get the program, and get the fund started? What will be gained by postponing it for six months? Absolutely nothing.
Improvements can be made to the legislation in committee. This can be done by having discussions with those groups directly affected. We can certainly improve the legislation by experience in the utilization of it. The first

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-41 seems to me to be a very complex way of getting at a simple problem, its goal being to protect the western grain farmers' income. What we are really after is price and market insurance.
Although I have a great deal of respect for the intelligence of the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, I sometimes wonder about his common sense. I feel the bill before us is lacking in what could be called an approach of common sense. That is why we in the Conservative Party feel its subject-matter should be referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture before we proceed with second reading. In that way we would be able to hear those who wish to make representations before the bill passes second reading.
The purpose of Bill C-41, the grain stabilization bill, is to provide for stabilization of the net proceeds from the production and sale of western grain and to protect the producer from the ups and downs of the prices, and the quantities that move into the international market. This is as opposed to a crop insurance plan, which looks after the vagaries of Mother Nature.
It is generally conceded that by confining ourselves to practical farming methods already used by good farmers in different parts of the world, we could feed something like ten times our present population, and on a Canadian style of diet. This can be done only if the profit incentive is there for farmers to take the risk inherent in agriculture and to increase their output and productivity. But this must not be limited by the actions of the government.
The first question on this bill, of course, is: do we really need this new scheme for grain at this time, or is there some alternative course that we should take? The concept may be valid, and it may be needed for products such as eggs and fruit. But the question is: will it be administrable for grain without creating a bureaucratic structure that could overwhelm us? It is not the concept of the grain stabilization plan that is complex and unattractive; it is the operational and administrative features that require understanding.
It would seem, on looking through the notes on the western grain stabilization working paper put out by the government, that the main selection of criteria used was the cheapest plan for a given level of stability, and a plan that is actuarially sound. This, of course, in no way argues
Western Grain Stabilization
that it is an optimum plan for either government or producers.
The key question becomes: what stability is really provided to commercial western grain producers, and at what cost? That is, what are the costs and benefits from such a program compared to alternatives?
From the latest figures I have looked at, we can expect that about one-half of the commercial grain sales in western Canada would be covered by the $25,000 gross sales limitation, and there is no evidence that farmers with sales of $25,000 or less are in greater need of grain stabilization as opposed to larger grain farmers. Again, if the plan is actuarially sound, why use the $25,000 limit?
The bill appears to take the narrow view that the government is giving out money benevolently to provide some stabilization, and the level of the gift is the key focus. There are, however, direct and indirect benefits that the government receives as well as the farmers. For example, if a stabilizing net cash flow payment occurs, there is likely to be a four to five times multiplier effect on the prairie economy, and assuming standard tax levels it would seem the federal government would get back anywhere from $1.25 to $1.75 for every dollar it pays out. There is also the question of whether federal financial authorities might attempt or be able to deduct such payments from federal transfer payments to the provinces.
The point is that the program is unlikely to have a net cost to government at all, and therefore, as I said before, why have the $25,000 gross sales limit? Larger farm spending could be expected to have similar multiplier effects, so the question is: is the middle-size farmer the appropriate structural objective for western grain stabilization?
There can be lots of questions raised about entry, reentry, and getting out later, who administers the program, who pays for the administrative cost. One might also ask about the three-year system of calculating individual payout, which seems to penalize those producers who are expanding compared with those who are stable or are reducing.
So we go back to the first question: do we need this scheme? Certainly it was needed 20 years ago. However, when we look to the future, there are some questions. What we need now is a list of priorities. I suggest that labour disputes, transportation, high taxation, high interest rates, must be right at the top.
I personally think the alternative to this plan would be a crop insurance program administered by each of the western provinces, and we have a good basis for that now. We need a plan to take into account regional differences in the Canadian Wheat Board area, such as climate and soil type. This bill deals with the prairie economy as a whole.
Another danger to a plan such as Bill C-41 is that it tends to shelter the farmer from the marketplace. It is another block between the producer and the realities of the marketplace. There should be some provision for reassessing this program after three or five years. We can ask if farm-to-farm sales are to be excluded. Certainly, eastern grain producers will wonder about this plan. Are they interested in this scheme? What about grain fed on the farm? Does this qualify? There is no question that the economists who dreamed up this scheme have been look-

May 5, 1975
Western Grain Stabilization
ing back, and that it is based on the past 25 years. Surely we can reasonably expect the next 25 years to be better for agriculture, so I very much question the actuarial basis, especially when the two key areas are Mother Nature and people.
One thing this bill will do: it will be a real red herring to cool the whole transportation and grain situation for the government. It will keep the farmers busy all summer trying to figure it out.
I am not aware of any producer pressure for this scheme. As I said before, we seem to be overwhelmed with pressing problems in the grain industry. I would like to see some of these solved before we move into these unknown waters. They include grain transportation, rail line abandonment, improved facilities on the Pacific seaboard and at Churchill, protein payment, development of a soft white wheat, a Chief Commissioner for the Canadian Wheat Board, a farm storage program, a government grain storage program, some tax relief, a registered retirement savings plan for farmers or ranchers, solutions to labour strife and industrial disputes, some effective chemical control for insects and wild oats, and general measures to prevent rural depopulation. When we consider the magnitude of past errors of judgment in the western grain industry there is room for lots of searching research here.
In closing I strongly recommend that the House support the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Grenville Carleton (Mr. Baker), so that the committee may be able to travel and in order that western farmers themselves can supply input to this legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of speaking a second time on this bill as a consequence of the amendment. I hope the House will support the amendment; I appeal to members on the opposite side to do so.
I think most of us will agree that there is throughout the farm organizations, and certainly among farmers all across Canada, a desire to establish for themselves an income stabilization policy. Such a policy can be established in two or three ways.
One of the reasons why I am so interested in having the subject matter of the bill referred to committee is that I have little hope in the minister's response to suggestions to improve legislation of his in committee, regardless of what the evidence proves. There is little chance of acceptance of change by the minister.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) who has just taken his seat. I was pleased to note there was no rancor on his part regarding the minister and stabilization. I think the last time there was any agricultural stabilization he and his party members in western Canada felt the effects. If you remember, Mr. Speaker, at that time we were faced with a much more comprehensive bill than the one we have now; it was a $100 million carrot held out in Saskatchewan for election purposes.
The situation then was not much different from what it is now since an election will probably take place there this year. It was nice to have a bill just before the last election

there so that the election could be fought on better ground.
I agree that this bill is a better bill by a considerable margin than the previous bill, but I would suggest to the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley that stabilization and the huge carrot held out last time were not to the advantage of his own party.
I was also surprised to hear the hon. member mention a matter that has not been referred to in the House for some time, and that is the bootlegging of grain. I was particularly surprised to hear him bring that subject up, knowing that he had been a cabinet minister in the Thatcher government at a time when most members of parliament here in Ottawa were of the opinion that the biggest bootlegger in Saskatchewan was Mr. Thatcher, the premier, who traded wheat for furniture and built up quite a bootlegging business. Not that there is anything wrong with bootlegging, Mr. Speaker, but it is a page in our history that we look back to and hope that it will remain in the past. As I say, I was surprised to hear the hon. member raise the subject, particularly in view of the connection it must have had with some of the people with whom he was fairly close.
The last time the stabilization bill came before the House no consultation was held with farm organizations and farmers. A number of economists and officials in the various departments concerned with the marketing of grain drafted a program in which a number of programs already in effect were eliminated. Most of them had been unsuccessful, with the possible exception of PFAA, which still has a fund of $9 million which is to be put to use under the terms of this bill. But with that one exception, none of these other carrots ever produced any advantage for the farmers.
It should also be pointed out that not only was an election fought and the stabilization act lost, but some court cases followed in which it was charged that in order to make his point the minister was doing things which were dishonest and illegal. It was amusing to see the minister recommending an illegality to accomplish a political end, yet this was the decision of the court, and at that time stabilization was dead.
At that time other matters were mentioned, one of which was cost of production indexing. The minister gave no consideration to that at all because it did not fit in with the nice, neat little bill that he had drafted. It might have interfered in some way with the structure that had been established. If the subject of this bill is referred to committee, it would be my expectation and hope that we would hear from farm organizations, those connected with the trade, and others. The subject matter of the bill does not only concern the farmers: as someone has mentioned, it also concerns the grain exchange, those brokers who travel across the world to sell our cereal products, those who are concerned with the tariff structure and the relationship between our exports and imports, as well as a very large segment of the Canadian economy, since wheat and cereal grains play such an important role in the export capacity of this nation. The effects of the bill spread far beyond those who just produce the grain.
If the subject matter of the bill is referred to committee we would be able to listen to the input of those who come before us. This would be before the bill was finally draft-
May 5, 1975

ed, and before the minister's position had become so inflexible that he could not possibly change anything in the bill without losing face. If there is one thing this minister does not like, it is to lose face by changing something.
The backbenchers in the Liberal party who are from farming districts know that this bill can be improved. It is not the only answer to stabilization. They know there are other factors that the farmers will put before the committee for consideration, and which have not yet been discussed. As the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has already done, farm organizations will probably give an indication that there are two forms of assistance that can be provided to give income stability, only one of which is outlined in the present bill.
I suggest that the whole country is going to be affected by this piece of legislation, not only this year but for many years to come. Unless we are to believe that the cabinet has all of the knowledge, that the farmers have none, that the farm organizations have none, and yes that, even individual members of parliament have none, then I would strongly urge the Liberal party, and its members particularly from western Canada, to vote against sending the subject matter of the bill to committee-in other words, to vote against the amendment. In the standing committee they will obviously be able to use their majority and will eventually get their way; it only becomes a matter of time. If that is what they wish, then obviously they should be opposed to sending the subject matter to a committee.
If they believe that such things as the stabilization of income for cereal producers in Canada, and its relationship to export and domestic sales of wheat and other cereals, with the effect this will have on production of livestock in western Canada and on any attempt to diversify production away from cereal grains in given areas of western Canada, are not important, then obviously they will vote against the amendment and will not send the subject matter of the bill to committee. However, if they feel this is a long-term proposition that is worth looking into, then I would strongly urge them to send the subject matter to committee.
I suggest that we are discussing a bill that is highly technical. We must first decide what type of stabilization we want. The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) said that no one else had set out an alternative. That is true. It would take considerable effort to do so. I give the minister full credit for having made that effort. Certainly the effort that has gone into the development of this piece of legislation has been considerable. This is probably a technically correct bill. The question I raise is whether it is correct as far as the agricultural community in western Canada is concerned, and that is what we would be discussing if we discussed the subject matter instead of the bill.
The Federation of Agriculture put out a paper on farm income protection. Its convention passed a fairly simple resolution which states in part;
Whereas provincial farm income protection plans are emerging as an approach to farm income stabilization and protection
Western Grain Stabilization
Be it resolved that the C.F.A. endorses the concept, and establishes the principle that the farmers of Canada must occupy a position in Canadian society that generally provides to farmers, net income and conditions of work at least equal to those conditions and incomes in society as a whole in terms of return to investment, managerial ability, hours of work and conditions of employment; and
Be it further resolved that the C.F.A. work to achieve national commodity income protection plans with a minimum of adjustment being required; and
Be it further resolved that any plan or plans meet at least the following policy.
To provide a price guarantee for farmers during periods of unfavourable market conditions based on cost of production.
The federation went on to set forth a number of methods. Having seen the legislation which is put forth, the federation outlined a number of alternatives to what is presented in this bill. What is being presented in this bill is really subsidization with the co-operation of the farmers and the government. When the prices fall and remain down over a period of time, the government makes a contribution.
Of course there are other types of protection. Most of the provinces, including British Columbia and Quebec, are looking very closely at another type which involves the cost of production, a reasonable wage for the entrepreneur and labour costs, all of which things would be reflected in the price in the marketplace.
British Columbia is operating this type of a program on the basis of allowing the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture to establish prices for commodities, which involves a detailed look at what they call model farm units. This is done through a negotiating agreement committee which makes a study in depth when establishing the cost of production. That is the way the province of British Columbia is handling income stabilization. This allows a great deal of flexibility and an orderly increase in the production of specific commodities as the ability to sell the commodity increases.
That federation is not in favour of establishing production quotas or controls which will regulate the degree of participation by individual farmers, or will place limitations on production. Personally I would like to go a step further in deciding how much of a product can be sold, and at what price. We should also calculate the cost of production.
When I hear people talk about stabilization and the danger of over-production I am reminded of what happens when you get a very good or a very low price for a commodity. I am reminded of earlier days working in a mine when we had a change from a 10-hour day to an 8-hour day. Many of the employees were asked, and agreed to work an extra two hours a day in order to get the extra money they needed. They felt the way to get this extra money was to work an extra couple of hours. They had done it before, so they wondered why they should not go back to the 10-hour day.
We did not let them work the 10 hours a day. We had established that an 8-hour day was sufficient. We decided that just because they could not earn the money they needed by working an 8-hour day there was no point in working the extra two hours. We felt it was much better to bring the pay up so the 8-hour day would produce a decent

income for those people. I think labour in general has taken that attitude.
We have been using a number of federal programs to stabilize agricultural products. I think anyone who is remotely connected with agriculture will agree that one of the bright spots in the history of agriculture was the stabilization of dairy products. This was not accomplished without difficulty. Some small dairy farmers have gone out of business. Cream production is non-existent in many parts of the country. In the main, dairy production has been stabilized and the prices have kept relatively level.
I suggest that if this industry had not been regulated and there had not been a willingness to put the right amount of money into the program at the right time, we might have been faced with one of two things. We would either have over-produced and had lower prices, or overproduced and had to buy the excess commodity with government funds, as we have always done in the past. This was not necessary because we were judicial in deciding on what the optimum prices should be. The government must be given full credit for having done this. This was done on a national basis, but it has not been an easy proposition. I think all those connected with the dairy industry will agree that it was only successful because all the farmers agreed to participate in the program.
You will find in Ontario, I am sure, that the majority of farmers will agree that industrial milk prices have been advantageously raised to a level that has not destroyed the fluid milk industry. In fact it has supplemented the fluid milk industry by making it possible for that industry to obtain a large source of supply. At the same time it has enabled the industry to provide good products to the consumers at reasonable prices.
If this stabilization bill is to be successful we will require the participation of all producers of the commodities involved. Unless we have that input to a program that is acceptable, it will not work. I am surprised to hear members in this House, particularly those on the government side, suggest that this program is not too good, that it is flexible and allows room for change, and that it will be changed shortly. I suggest that we should start off with an optimum amount of input from the farmers.
We should not look only to the bright little boys in government departments who may have a very good plan, but one which is totally unrealistic to the farmers who do the producing. While it sounds complicated to me I am sure those people who use a slide rule or calculator do not find the calculations difficult. However, the fact is that the farmer must know how it is done so that he will know whether or not he is satisfied. Any information I have is that the farmers have not been consulted at all. The last occasion was in 1971 and at that time they were very strongly opposed to it, even with the carrot of $100 million. Facsimiles of the cheques were sent out telling them how much they would receive. They still turned it down.
I think it is wrong for us to talk about the concept of agricultural stabilization in the cereal field at this time without having the full input of the farming community. We have not had a major farm conference for some time. I think we had one about ten years ago. At that time the
[Mr. Peters.)
farmers came down here and set forth a number of proposals which the government has been attempting to implement ever since, even though many of them are out of date.
It seems to me that if we do not have this kind of input from the farmers who are directly concerned, we will not have a stabilization plan that will be acceptable. Surely as members of parliament that is what we wish. If one looks around the various departments of the government one will see many whizz-kids of 22 or 25 years of age who are just recently out of university. There are many of these very bright young people in government departments. They are very competent in their fields, but they have one great disability. They lack experience. One cannot hold that against them because they will gain experience as they become older.
Most of us who are members of parliament have some limited experience, and should be in a position to adopt a program which we believe is the ultimate. Surely we want the best plan to stabilize income for agriculture. We are quickly running out of farmers. It has been mentioned that the average age of a farmer is well over 50.
Recently I witnessed a sad event. It involved a farm that was started up by a chap who came to the country when it was opened up. The son of this original farmer, who is now on in years and who has farmed for many years, has two sons of his own. The farm is a good operation. It has all the necessary livestock, implements, and necessities for farming. But this farmer sold the farm because the two sons took a look at it and said that they could get more money by working in a machine shop or in other employment off the farm. They said they would have every Saturday and Sunday off, and a number of paid holidays. They said that in this way they could take a few days off without being hurt too badly financially, and without allowing the cows to suffer. So we do not get young people on the farms.
This farm was sold to a buyer from Toronto who intends to hold it strictly for speculation purposes. He has offered to rent it to another farmer for the next year or two because he does not anticipate selling it again in that period. He has also bought eight or ten other farms.

We are really are not discussing the bill. We are discussing an amendment to send the whole problem of farm income stabilization to the committee without the bill, so that the subject may be discussed and representations heard in order to decide whether or not this is the kind of bill we should be implementing in respect of stabilization. I was indicating that the need for farm stabilization is obvious in view of the lack of income in the farming community today, which has resulted in very few young people going into agriculture.
May 5, 1975

The age of the average farmer now is increasing well beyond the half century in years, and unless we get additional farmers we will have serious difficulty not only in this particular field but in all fields directly related to agricultural production. I am sure the minister's advisers would agree that this bill is only one form of stabilization. The minister, of course, will argue that it is the ideal one for this purpose. The purpose of the amendment, however, is to have the subject matter, which is really grain income stabilization, sent to committee so that we may ascertain whether or not this is the proper route or whether another route might be suggested.
I have indicated I am doubtful that the minister will agree we should look at other forms of income stabilization, but I suggest we have already in the past looked at two, three, or four types of income stabilization in the agricultural field. The other stabilization bill involves a totally different method, and I am sure there are also others.
I have not spoken at all of the method that was used in the other stabilization bill. One form of that of course is deficiency payments, where the marketplace is allowed to play the full role and at the end of the year you calculate on your political basis, or your cost of production basis, or however you wish, the need of the producer in respect of that particular commodity to have a certain amount of money, and if the price of that commodity in the open market is not sufficiently high a deficiency payment is made almost always on a subsidization basis without any regard to premium paid by the producer. There are also other methods.
On a number of occasions we have used named commodities and have agreed that a commodity would be pegged at a level that would be a percentage of the actual cost of production and what would be necessary to keep the producer in business. In those instances we have made an offer of a percentage of the cost of production of the commodity, and have said that any amount they wish to produce we would buy. This has been done on a number of occasions, and in fact the largest expenditure in agriculture has always been in stabilization under the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
On numerous occasions we have obtained large quantities of surplus products which we had to dispose of eventually, often at a considerable loss to the nation. In all those cases, when the cost of production increases rapidly, to raise prices to the same level becomes futile because the input in production is usually considerably higher than the increase in the cost of the product. This is one of the major problems that we have to face, and we must face this problem in almost any type of stabilization program that we put into effect.
If this bill were in effect today and prices started to drop, the payment we would be making would be very high, but the income level would be dropping and we would be paying a premium on that loss to the farmer at the same time that his input cost for the production of the commodity was going up rapidly.
It is normal, when prices are low and income is based on a five year or any other average, that when prices start to
Western Grain Stabilization
increase farmers continue to have yet higher input costs. So that when the price of the product is low, input prices continue to go up and are never below the five year average. The farmer will be paying premiums, but he will not get any benefits because the market price may be going up gradually.
It seems to me that there are a number of ways in which the problem of stabilization can be solved. This is a very important subject, probably the most important subject that agriculture has ever faced. Farmers do not have the advantage of the strike weapon, they cannot withhold their product from the market. Also, it is impossible to organize a boycott among farmers. I remember one time when, in an effort to get a better price for fluid milk, producers organized a meeting at which they discussed what they needed to do to stay in business. I suggested to them that the way to go about it would be to dump their milk, thus creating a shortage on the market. Immediately the farmers asked, who will pay for the milk?
When a labourer goes on strike, he knows who will pay for it-he will. But when the farmer was asked to withhold his product-

It seems to me that that is not the way in which prices can be maintained by Canadian farmers, that withholding their products is not the right way. I am sure every member of the House is well aware of the fact that if farmers adopted that method, there would be a shortage of food in all parts of Canada and we would all suffer.
Farmers should have no complaints about the actions of Canadians in general with regard to them because the Canadian population has been willing to support agriculture, and on many occasions to stabilize farmers' incomes. They have done so gladly and without reluctance. In return, farmers have had to pay a very severe price, namely, a loss in their income.
In bringing forward this legislation the minister has put forth a method by which grain production can be stabilized. It is true that it has many variables and that large sectors of producers in western Canada might find themselves making no deliveries and no sales. Yet, under this bill, if the other areas receive a good price for their commodity, a price which meets the criteria established in the bill, then no pay-out takes place anywhere. It is possible that if grain production is good in Assiniboia, in the Palliser triangle, and in other extremely productive wheat producing areas where number 1 wheat is the rule rather than the exception, the remaining three quarters of the prairie region which on many occasions produce substandard grain whether it be because of frost, hail, or grasshoppers, will get nothing for their product.
