speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words in the debate on Bill C-41. I was not in the House when the minister introduced the bill, but I did have the opportunity to read his speech. I hope he did not strain his arm as he patted himself on the back for the programs and planning he claims he has developed or is developing to put grain farmers on the road to prosperity.
Bill C-41 is entitled: "An act respecting the stabilization of net proceeds from the production and sale of western grain ...". The history of grain production in the west is one of instability in the thirties and the early forties, caused by drought and grasshoppers. These were acts of God. There was really no means by which the producer could control those hazards. Since then, while there have been dry periods and hoppers, there have been new developments in the field of farm machinery, there are new farming practices, new chemicals to control weeds and hoppers, and these have enabled the farmer to increase his grain production so much that the annual average yield per acre has increased over the long term average by as much as 10 or 15 bushels per acre in some areas.
In the last 10 or 15 years we have been producing a substantial amount of grain every year, with the exception of the year we had the LIFT program. Basically, production is not really the problem in the west. Our problems are primarily man made. They are problems of inadequate or poorly planned transportation systems, labour disputes, strikes both with the railway company on the west coast 
and amongst the longshoremen, and a lack of salesmanship. If we can solve these problems that will take most of the instability out of grain production in the west. We must solve these problems.
The lack of an international wheat agreement has and will continue to lead to instability. Many parts of the world are faced with starvation. Surely as a producer of cereal crops it is Canada's responsibility to help feed the starving world. I am not suggesting that we give this grain away, but I am wondering what we as Canadians have done to work out an international wheat agreement with other producing countries of the world. What are we doing to make satisfactory financial arrangements with some of the underdeveloped countries in order to help them in their plight?
As the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) said, the bill before us is complicated. I sometimes wonder who drafts the legislation which is presented. When I started practising law some 20 years ago one could pick up the statutes of Canada, or the statutes of any of the provinces, and any layman could read those statutes and understand them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: You've got to be kidding.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: This is a fact, if you will go back that far.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: Did you ever read the Succession Duty Act?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Yes. It is fairly simple compared to the legislation before us. Every piece of legislation I have seen come into this House since 1972 has been complicated. The only legislation I have seen in the last three years which a layman could understand is the Corporations Act. Someone with some sense drafted that legislation.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton read clause 6 of the bill. That clause is simple compared to clauses 9 to 11 inclusive. When I first saw the bill I did a careful study of it, and I did relatively well in understanding what it meant until I reached clauses 9 to 11. I sat down with a pencil and paper, as did many of my colleagues, in an attempt to try to understand what those clauses meant, and it seems to me that unless one has a computer or has studied higher mathematics, it is an impossibility to understand what it is all about.
Perhaps the minister has access to a computer or to someone who has studied higher mathematics. He did give some examples in his speech in the House. He spoke about benefits if the plan had started in 1965 and carried on until 1975. He spoke of the amount of benefits a producer would receive for the period 1968 to 1971. Presumably he was working on the basis that the producer had contributed the maximum for the years 1966, 1967 and 1968. But what would the payment be to the farmer if we started in 1975 and the net cash flow for each of the next three years was below the five year average? This is something hon. members should know, and something members of farm organizations and individual farmers should know so that they can study the bill and understand it.
There has been the suggestion by hon. members on this side of the House that the stabilization bill should be tied into the Crop Insurance Act. The minister has said that this is impossible. I believe that it is possible and that it
May 5, 1975

can easily be done. It needs some study, perhaps, but I sincerely believe that the matter of combining the stabilization bill with the Crop Insurance Act should be seriously considered.
The bill as it stands covers the whole of the Canadian Wheat Board area. I can visualize many areas over the years where no payment will be made under this legislation where there will be crop failures, perhaps due to isolated areas of drought, hoppers, Bertha Army Worms and other problems, but the Wheat Board area as a whole will have an income which will prevent payment out to these areas.
It will be like the PFAA program when for many years it worked on the block system. There were many instances where farmers with good crops received benefits because the average of the area they were in was low. There were neighbours across the fence who had no crops year after year, but they were in an area where the average was high, and they received no payment. I know, because I lived on a farm which was on the wrong side of the fence.
I submit that the administrative machinery is in place under the Crop Insurance Act to administer a program such as this. The minister has not told us what it will cost to administer this legislation. Will there be a duplication of inspectors? Will the inspectors under the Crop Insurance Act come to the farm one day, and will the inspectors under the stabilization program come to the farm the next day to measure the same bin and perhaps arrive at a different figure? I see the minister smiling.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member can tell me how he develops the fear that any bin measuring is required at all. As I read the bill, everything depends upon the sales of grain. speechtext: In response to the minister, Madam Speaker, I would point out that the bill calls for a year end inventory, and it would seem to me that an inventory would require the measurement of the grain on the farm.

speechtext: Nonsense.

speechtext: Where is it?

speechtext: It is not in the bill.

speechtext:
Unless the bill has been changed since it was first presented or since I last read it-in any event,
Western Grain Stabilization
Madam Speaker, I do not have the time now to read the bill through, but I will be happy to dig out the particular section and send a note across to the minister later.
I wonder if the minister is afraid to combine this stabilization plan with the crop insurance program. Is he concerned that, because the crop insurance is administered provincially and the stabilization plan will be administered federally, the provinces will get the credit?
Stabilization of income for the western grain farmer is important and essential. It is important that the program be effective and not one that just tosses out a few dollars to the farmer, particularly at election time. I think that the bill should be referred to committee for study and that the minister and officials of his department should appear and give open and frank answers to questions raised by the committee. That information should be fed back to farm organizations and individual farmers. There must be thoughtful study in order that the plan may be workable if it is adopted.
It must be a plan that is as free as possible of red tape, and it must give real stability. It must also be a plan that the producer wants, and that he is satisfied with. It must not be forced upon the producer in the west, because he is an independent person who wants to make his own decisions and not be dictated to by anyone. He is suspicious of government and suspicious of bureaucrats-and who can blame him?
A producer in my riding handed me a news report from the Western Producer of April 10 when I was home last week, which reads as follows:
Wheat Board Commissioner R.M. Esdale announced April 4 that all quotas on durum and the top three grades of red spring wheat will be open until May 16, when they will terminate.
Mr. Esdale said the quota changes are necessary to ensure that remaining on-farm supplies of high-grade wheat are delivered into the elevator system between now and mid-May, to meet immediate export requirements at both east and west coast positions.
"With the recent resumption in export shipments out of the west coast and Thunder Bay, every effort must be made to compensate for the delays we have experienced over the past few months," the commissioner said. "This means that the grain needed to fulfil sales commitments must be moved forward as quickly as possible."
The producer told me that he had the grain, and would like to deliver despite the fact that he was in the process of getting his machinery and his farm ready to seed. But the roads have a ban on them, Madam Speaker. The provincial government will not permit the trucks to travel on the highways, so he cannot deliver. He asks, "Am I to be cut off at May 16 and not allowed to deliver any more grain?" The western grain producer does not take kindly to threats, Madam Speaker. He was threatened by the minister under the LIFT program and told, "Cut back on your grain production or you will have a cutback on your quota." In this case it is, "Deliver by May 16 or you will be cut off-you cannot deliver any more grain this crop year".
The western grain producer is a smart businessman. If left alone and not threatened, not given bad advice, he can operate a good and efficient business. He, and he alone, can tell this government and this minister what kind of stabilization program he needs and what type of program will be efficient. Let us give him a chance to have an input.

May 5, 1975
Adjournment Debate
We are asking that this bill be not now read a second time but be referred back to the committee in order that the individual producer and the farm organizations can have an input. The committee should travel. There is no point in a committee meeting only in Ottawa and, only organizations appearing before it; there must be the individual input as well.
I would therefore ask, Madam Speaker, that members on both sides of the House support the motion of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker).

speechtext: Madam Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the amendment now before the House-

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: It is a filibuster.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
When the hon. member speaks of filibuster it seems that Liberal members of this House of Commons are so eager to get legislation passed that they forget the purpose of parliament. Parliament is to represent the democracy we still have in Canada.
The amendment which is proposed commends itself to all members of this House. When one studies the track record of this piece of legislation-and I say this to the new members who were not here in 1971-one realizes that the farmers were actually saved money in 1971 by parliament not passing the bill that was then before the House. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board is a great mathematician, so if I am wrong in that statement I am sure he will rise tomorrow and prove it. But I know he cannot, Madam Speaker.
In 1971 the House of Commons saved money for the farmer by not passing a piece of legislation similar to that which is before us now. If the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board had brought in operation LIFT as legislation instead of by order in council and regulations, members who were here at that time could have saved the farmers' money by opposing and defeating that legislation. The minister did not have the farmers' point of view when he brought in that earlier legislation.
May I call it ten o'clock, Madam Speaker.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RESTRUCTURE RELATIONS WITH DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RESTRUCTURE RELATIONS WITH DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if we have learned anything in the past year, especially from conferences conducted by the United Nations on the subjects of energy, population, food and the Law of the Sea, it is that all of these problems are not

diminished but are interlocked and required an interlocking solution.
It is no longer enough for us to consider unilateral solutions to problems which cross national frontiers and are global in character. We need a comprehensive policy by the countries known as the developed countries, in which we bring together reforms of our trade and international monetary arrangements, our foreign aid programs- all of these things must come together. I think this is one of the things we have learned.
It is not enough for us just to consider CIDA, important as that agency is, and which the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence is now considering. Certainly CIDA needs to be investigated and there are things which the committee needs to highlight, but it is wrong to think that only an examination of CIDA is enough to repair the damage done to the poor nations or the world.
Today I put a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), who has just returned after acting in his capacity as chairman of the International Monetary Fund. I asked him about the situation concerning the recovery of the industrialized nations, the rich nations of the west, from the excessive prices that we have had to pay as a result of the quadrupled oil costs of the past year or 18 months, because the International Monetary Fund reported that the industrialized nations have been able in this very short space of time to come back. We have recovered.
The minister responded to me that the situation with the poor countries of the third world is still desperate. It is as it was before. That illustrates my point. Despite all the CIDA aid and other aid of the developed countries to the developing countries, that aid was wiped out because of the escalation of energy costs which has resulted in those countries being unable to buy sufficient fertilizer. It has led directly to famine situations in Africa, India, Bangladesh and other countries of Asia. In short, what do we have?
I wish to quote from a brief presented to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence from the Canadian Council for International Cooperation. I
quote:
No real solution of the food problem can be found unless fundamental social reforms are initiated that will allow the weak nations to share with the powerful in political power and the control of resources. In some way, CIDA could become the government indicator showing the way toward a new international economic order. Along the same line, non-governmental organizations are convinced that they can contribute new thinking. But, to this end, it would be necessary to cut the ties of dependency of the poor on the rich, and recognize that external aid can no more be considered the primary element of Canadian policy toward the third world.
That is where we are now. That is why I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) back in March if he would support the suggestion of a permanent sub-committee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to consider international development because of the need for a long-range comprehensive policy that gets us beyond just foreign aid. The Prime Minister said at that time he would welcome suggestions and input from all members of the House. When I put the same question to
May 5, 1975

the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) in committee, he said he would not oppose it.
Because of the special session on development which the United Nations will hold in September when these problems will come into their proper focus, and this is something for which Canada is now preparing a special policy stand, the time has come for the members of this House to share in the development of a Canadian policy that will reflect a comprehensive way in which the Canadian government can take a leadership role internationally to do that which will go beyond what we have done this far.
I believe the members of that committee are ready to move in this direction. I believe that would be the most constructive way in which we could help to reduce the dependency of the poor countries on the rich countries.
There must be new structures worked out for social reform. It is not enough just to have an interdepartmental committee on economic relations with developing countries. That is quite a mouthful. It is a committee of officials from the various government departments who are meeting to draw up this comprehensive policy about which I am speaking. It is not enough just to have officials from the various departments concerned with Canada's new role internationally, about which the Prime Minister is speaking at the Commonwealth Conference and about which the Secretary of State for External Affairs is speaking.
There are members on the external affairs committee who want to share in the development of the Canadian policy. We can do the same kind of job that was done when there was the special committee on international development at the time of the total foreign policy review in 1970. Many things have changed throughout the world in the short space of five years. We now see the hopelessness of single actions by countries which are not responding to the full approach of the United Nations' desire for a comprehensive policy. This is the way Canada can move ahead.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RESTRUCTURE RELATIONS WITH DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to respond on behalf of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Breau) to the question from the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) concerning co-operation between the developed countries and the developing countries of the third world. This is certainly a very appropriate time for such a matter to be raised having regard to the role and activity of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the Commonwealth Conference now going on in the Caribbean.
The concern of the government to ensure that developing countries are able to derive greater benefits from their participation in international trade, investment and finance was indicated very well in the Speech from the Throne where it was stated that Canada's contribution would involve us not only in increasing the flow of financial assistance through developing countries but also in re-examining other policies which affect our economic relations with the third world. The Prime Minister reiterated this concern in London.
Adjournment Debate
The interdepartmental committee on economic relations with developing countries was established by ministers at the suggestion of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) to carry out the re-examination of those other policies which affect our economic relations with developing countries. The policies in question fall in the areas of tariffs and trade, investment, the provision of appropriate technology, and financial and monetary policy. They may also touch on questions of transport, energy, resources and agricultural development. The committee is pursuing a continuing review of these policies from the perspective of the bearing they have on Canada's over all relationship with developing countries.
A number of international meetings in the future, at which issues of importance to the developing countries will be discussed, will afford Canada the opportunity to consult with both developing and developed countries with a view to taking appropriate action to respond to the needs and aspirations of developing countries.

subtopic: MANPOWER-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-PROPOSED CONTROL OF GRANTS ON A CONSTITUENCY BASIS
MANPOWER-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-PROPOSED CONTROL OF GRANTS ON A CONSTITUENCY BASIS
speechtext:
I rise tonight to follow up a question I put to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) on March 24 concerning the Opportunities for Youth program. My question was:
Given the fact that the consideration and granting of OFY grants through the use of management area advisory groups is suffering from a lack of information, advice, control, and any indication of managerial competence on the part of his department, is the minister giving consideration to allotment and control of OFY grants on a local constituency basis where the advisory group would at least have some knowledge of the project being considered?
At this point the record reads:

subtopic: MANPOWER-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-PROPOSED CONTROL OF GRANTS ON A CONSTITUENCY BASIS
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
I might say that the hon. members who applauded my question were mainly Liberal backbenchers. The minister replied-I will excerpt parts of what he said:
We do not have the sound statistical base in such detail as to be usable for OFY allocations at the constituency level.... From that stems the problem of having to make allocations in a broader geographical area, such as labour management areas where the consultation process takes place. Also, it was a choice between giving hon. members the opportunity to name people with whom we would consult or arbitrarily, as in the past, have the people with whom to consult in the community selected by the departmental staff.
This is an attempt to excuse a shocking method of dispensing public public funds. I am reminded of the days when Jimmy Walker of New York City was caught the same way. His reply then was: "There comes a time in politics when a man must rise above principle." This seems to me to be what the minister was attempting to do.
Last fall or winter I received a direction from the minister to select two members for this advisory committee from among my constituents, and I did so. Another direction was that one member should be under 25 years of age, and I was fortunate to be able to select two very competent people. This administrative area group comprised five constituencies. We expected there would be ten delegates or members of the committee. I found out, somewhat

May 5, 1975
Adjournment Debate
to my surprise, that there were the two from my constituency, one from Esquimalt-Saanich, none from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, none from Comox-Alberni, and none from Coast-Chilcotin. So this group was filled in by the Department of Manpower which appointed delegates that it knew, and the members it appointed were largely those people who had had OFY projects the previous year.
The pair that I sent to the committee meetings came back to me somewhat horrified after the first or second meeting and said that fantastic things were going on. There was, to them, this large amount of money, and to me it is a large amount of money, some $750,000, and they had not been given any advance notice or copies of the project summary sheets. Consequently, on the night of the first meeting they were handed hundreds of these sheets and were expected to start getting ready to make decisions regarding disbursements of taxpayers' money on this basis.
I could see no way out of it at that time so I encouraged these two people to continue going to the meetings, and they did so. But the difficulty was compounded by the enormous distances involved. For example, one constituency, that of Coast-Chilcotin, is on the mainland of B.C., and I suppose the closest point from my constituency is 80 to 100 miles away. Yet my representatives were expected to vote on projects submitted from Coast-Chilcotin without their knowing the people involved. In fact, they were fortunate if they knew the people involved in projects submitted from Victoria.
Let me point out that the summary sheets which they received, some of which I have, were models of brevity, certainly not models of any method known to mankind for giving information to other people. I have one in front of me. The name of the applicant does not matter, but this is the entire project description: "The objective of this project is to create a film on the concept of dance improvisation as an art form". I am told that there were five participants, the total work weeks involved amounted to 48, and the salaries to $5,280. With this scarcity of information the people on the OFY committee were expected to allocate funds. It is expected of the people who were appointed to these committees that they would give final advice on this kind of project.
It may be a great thing politically for the Liberal party to be able to disburse vast sums of money. But they need fall guys, and that is where we MP's come in, to take responsibility for the bad decisions. I suggested at one time that we should say we do not want any of this money so we can save the money of the taxpayers, but that just would not happen; the other four constituencies would get that many more projects. So our hands are tied. We cannot save the taxpayers' money, and we have to go along with this idiotic way of disbursing funds.
There may well be some good OFY projects; indeed I am sure there are. I have nothing against the basic concept of trying to get young people into the work force. They have a lot of good ideas, but how on earth are we expected to judge the good from the bad on the information provided? I have a booklet that lists the previous year's projects, but once again there is no information about whether any given project was any good or whether it was in fact

accomplished. All we know is that the money was paid out. The book contains hundreds of projects. For example, this is the one for Ganges:
Ganges-Salt Spring Youth Activity Centre (4X 1339) To provide a recreational and education experience for children on Salt Spring Island: $9,523; Jobs-12; Linda Stafford, Rainbow Road, 537-2937
The people on the committee could not tell whether that project was ever carried out, whether it was considered a good, bad, or indifferent project.
If the OFY is to go on, Madam Speaker, and to get the support of the community which the projects may well deserve, then we must have some kind of management procedures that will bear some resemblance to reality.

speakeroldname: Mr. William Rompkey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: MANPOWER-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-PROPOSED CONTROL OF GRANTS ON A CONSTITUENCY BASIS
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to reply to the hon. member. I should like to explain first of all why the management area advisory group system was introduced under this year's OFY program.
It had not been in existence before and was created as an offshoot really of the constituency advisory group instituted under the Local Initiatives Program. This type of consultation had been very successful, and it was thought that some sort of system like that would be appropriate under the OFY program. We needed to have community input and we needed to set up priorities, and we needed somebody who knew the local situation.
With regard to the comment of the hon. member that there were people on these advisory groups who had no knowledge of certain areas in which they were asked to make decisions, that of course was true. Then, of course, members of parliament are really in that same boat. An hon. member for British Columbia quite often has to make decisions in this parliament with regard to the Atlantic area, Quebec, or other areas of Canada with which he may not be totally familiar. In that sense I suppose democracy is a system which has faults, but is still the best system we have devised so far.
There may be refinements of the management advisory group, but this was an effort at least to involve local people in the decision making process. While it might not have been absolutely perfect, I believe it did have some sucess. It certainly did in my area, and the people I recommended to my own advisory groups I believe were quite satisfied that they were able to achieve what they set out to achieve.
Since the OFY program is aimed at a very special segment of the population it was deemed necessary to set up these advisory groups on the basis of management areas. As the minister said initially, we did not have the statistics available at the constituency offices to set up advisory groups in the same way we did with LIP.
Under the management advisory group system, representation can be made by people selected by the member of parliament and, of course, I should point out that an MP still gets the chance to make his own personal representations to the minister. If there should be somebody on the advisory group who does not know parts of the constituency, the MP having a knowledge of the whole constituency can make his representations to the minister on a very sound basis with very sound knowledge.
May 5, 1975

As the management area advisory group system is an experimental process, and because the program by its nature must operate within very restrictive time frames, some administration problems were to be expected. However, I would think that-

subtopic: POST OFFICE-ALLEGED LACK OF AUTHORITY FOR SALE OF NON-POSTAL ITEMS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
POST OFFICE-ALLEGED LACK OF AUTHORITY FOR SALE OF NON-POSTAL ITEMS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am at a bit of a loss to know whether I should commence my argument when there does not seem to be anybody on the other side to reply, although I received a note a few minutes ago from the hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore (Mr. Blaker) indicating that he might answer. If the Chair wishes I will proceed.
On Friday last I asked the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) a question concerning an operation of the Post Office, and I should like to read it into the record. It is: Since the Auditor General has again criticized the Post Office for selling non-postal items to the public without parliamentary authority, a practice which continues today, will the minister tell the House why this program was entered into without proper authorization and why suitable accounts had not been established to determine whether or not the program was profitable?
The minister replied on that day:
-a better authority on the subject is the deputy minister, who has appeared before the miscellaneous estimates committee to explain precisely the reasons for this. I assume the minutes are available. If I am wrong, I will find out for the hon. gentleman and report back on Monday.
At the time I was unable to ask a supplementary question which would have been in these terms: Why have steps not been taken to obtain the approval of this House for the program with which the Post Office is proceeding?
To give the House a little background I would point out that the Auditor General in his 1972 report first mentioned this problem. He referred to the marketing branch of the Post Office which had set up this program. The Auditor General said it involved the creation of 177 new positions, and was established in March 1971. He further stated that in addition to the sale of philatelic and other postal items the branch embarked upon a program of sales to the public of a number of miscellaneous items such as coin sets, commemorative spoons, and so on. He also observed that there are no established policies governing sales, inventories, or other facets of the activity.
Furthermore, he said whether or not the program was profitable in 1971-72 could not be determined as suitable accounts were not established for the activity, and over-all operating statements have not been prepared. The Auditor General suggested that the Deputy Postmaster General seek the opinion of the Department of Justice, and concluded his remarks by saying the department had included proposals for legislative action for the 1973 session by additional provisions in section 5 of the Act.
Adjournment Debate
A comment in terminology similar to that of the 1973 Auditor General's report appeared again in the 1974 report as follows:
We questioned whether this fell within the powers of the Postmaster General.
Then the report continued:
... it could not be determined whether the program was profitable since suitable accounts had not been established and over all operating statements had not been prepared.
It concluded:
A suitable financial reporting system to determine profitability by product has not yet been established ...
Three years in a row this situation has continued. The Deputy Minister appeared before the Public Accounts Committee and, although section 5 of the act gives wide powers to the Post Office but does not give the power to sell at retail non-postal items, the Deputy Minister suggested the section did give that power. There is no way a layman could interpret it in that manner.
Furthermore the minister said that a better authority is the Deputy Minister. Surely someone might argue that there is no better authority than the minister himself. The Deputy Minister told the Public Accounts Committee that he was afraid he could not answer on behalf of the Postmaster General. Now we have a minister telling the House that the best authority is the Deputy Minister, and the deputy minister is telling the committee that he cannot answer for the Postmaster General.
I should like to refer to the minutes of that committee for a moment. This meeting was held last Tuesday, April 29. The deputy minister admitted that their legislation did not cover the powers they were using, and said that they would in fact prepare legislation to be more specific concerning what this might mean. He went on to say that it is their intention to introduce a bill as soon as they can, and added that unfortunately he could not dictate government priority. Finally after persistent questioning he said it has not reached the House because it never reached bill stage.
He said the motive was profit. They wanted to reduce the deficit of the post office, in other words, produce a little profit. He actually said, "to increase the revenue which actually reduces the deficit". Well, now, it is obvious if one wants to produce a profit and determine whether or not one is producing a profit, one needs to provide the proper accounts. The Auditor General observed at the committee just last week that the Post Office was not authorized to do this anyway, and they agree with that. He continued by saying that there is no way to determine whether or not a loss is being incurred, but if a loss is being incurred he said he thinks it is fair to say this is an unauthorized drain on the public purse. The Public Accounts Committee in its fifth report stated:
... a government department should not initiate or take any action that is not authorized by Parliament even though it contemplates that Parliament may eventually take action to provide that authority. It considers that the actions of government departments must be limited at all times to the legislative authority existing at the time the action is taken.
If there were any doubts that the Post Office was continuing to carry on with this unauthorized practice, let me read from the most recent list of products the Post Office

subtopic: POST OFFICE-ALLEGED LACK OF AUTHORITY FOR SALE OF NON-POSTAL ITEMS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am happy to reply to the hon. member on behalf of the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) with regard to the selling of retail items through the Post Office. He has asked why the Post Office entered into these transactions. In 1970-71 when the Post Office embarked on a program of offering for sale certain items through some postal outlets, it did so in the belief that it had the authority under section 5 of the Post Office Act. I should like to read from that section which states:
5(1) Subject to this Act, the Postmaster General shall administer, superintend and manage the Canada Post Office, and without restricting the generality of the foregoing may-
(c) Establish and operate a system ... and such other services and
systems as he deems necessary or advisable for the efficient operation of the Canada Post Office.
Subsequently the Post Office encountered a difference of opinion with the Auditor General who took the approach that unless the Post Office had specific authority for these sales, it was in fact limited to the activities mentioned elsewhere in section 5.
In the interest of clarification, the Post Office proposed to introduce legislation which would set out specific authority for the sale of what it termed "postal related items". The nature of this legislation would be similar to that included in Bill C-196, an act respecting the 1976 summer Olympic games recently approved by parliament. This legislative amendment, however, was not regarded as a priority item by the government and has not yet been tabled for parliamentary consideration.
Since the Auditor General has registered his concern, the Canada Post Office has restricted its retail operations to convenience postal items related to its philatelic service, or encouraging better packaging, or supporting other government operations.
The government, in tabling proposals for legislative consideration, has devoted attention to matters that were regarded as having greater priority.
With regard to the adequate accounting system let me say that a system of accounting was not introduced which would reflect a full allocation of costs to these convenience items. The department considered that sales of these products would not result in an increase in overhead costs. Consequently the pricing on these convenience items during the initial period was limited to the direct or out of pocket costs plus a mark-up representing a contribution to overhead. The department has since taken steps to introduce an improved form of reporting.
